title: Short Stuff: 5 Lazarus Species
summary: Short Stuff episode on Lazarus species: animals thought to be extinct that were rediscovered. Covers the coelacanth (rediscovered off South Africa in 1938), the takahē of New Zealand (not seen for decades after the 1800s, rediscovered by Jeffrey Orbell in 1948), the Lord Howe Island stick insect (presumed extinct after rats from a shipwreck wiped it out, later found on nearby Pyramid Island in 1960, with a rodent eradication project underway), the Peruvian yellow-tailed woolly monkey (described in 1812, rediscovered in Brazil as a pet, with fewer than a thousand estimated in the wild), and Cope's robust redhorse (described in 1870, not seen for 122 years, rediscovered in the Savannah and Pee Dee rivers and bred in captivity). Also explains how the IUCN defines extinction.

entities.name: International Union for Conservation of Nature

segments.title: Opening and definition of Lazarus species
segments.summary: Hosts introduce five Lazarus species and define the term as an organism thought extinct that turns up alive again. They recap the coelacanth, rediscovered off South Africa, and tease the next animal.

segments.title: Takahē rediscovery
segments.summary: The takahē, a flightless New Zealand rail, was rare from the start. After a few specimens in the 1800s, a naturalist said further living birds were unlikely. Jeffrey Orbell searched for decades and found one in the South Island in 1948.

segments.title: How the IUCN declares extinction
segments.summary: The hosts explain that declaring a species extinct can be wrong because the world is large. The IUCN requires exhaustive surveys across the historic range before calling a species extinct.

segments.title: Lord Howe Island stick insect
segments.summary: Rats from a shipwreck overran Lord Howe Island and wiped out the tree lobster stick insect, which was thought extinct in the 1920s. Corpses found in 1960 showed a population survived on nearby Pyramid Island. A rodent eradication project using poison bait is underway.

segments.title: Peruvian yellow-tailed woolly monkey
segments.summary: The monkey was described in 1812 from a pelt and was seen only rarely afterward. It was presumed extinct until a specimen turned up as a pet in Brazil. Fewer than a thousand are estimated in the wild, and local Peruvians always knew it survived.

segments.title: Robust redhorse
segments.summary: Cope's robust redhorse was described in 1870 from one fish, which was later destroyed. It was not seen for 122 years, then reported in the Savannah and Pee Dee rivers. A captive breeding effort launched about twenty years ago led to wild juveniles from the restored population.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Hosts encourage listeners to look up more Lazarus species and sign off.
